extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys and agents), counsel handling USPTO disciplinary matters, and regulators/OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing professional conduct, fee handling, client communication, cooperation with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED), and sanctions for practitioners before the USPTO, as applied in an administrative disciplinary decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; the respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. The clear and convincing standard is intermediate between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt and requires evidence that produces a firm belief or conviction in the mind of the factfinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.49; case law guidance including Thomas v. Nicholson, Addington v. Texas, Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler, and Foster v. Alliedsignal. Defines 'clear' as certain/unambiguous/plain and 'convincing' as reasonable and persuasive enough to cause belief. Use this standard when assessing sufficiency of proof in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(1)-(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must: (1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance where the client's informed consent is required; (2) reasonably consult with the client about the means to accomplish the client's objectives; and (3) keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This communication duty makes the client part of decision-making. Failure to notify clients of time-sensitive Office Actions or Notices of Abandonment violates these provisions. Massachusetts Rule of Professional Conduct 1.4(a) tracks these duties; case example In re Haese shows failure to share financial decisions can violate the rule. Practitioners should notify clients of correspondence that could significantly affect a pending matter and solicit client input when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify client of correspondence that could have a significant effect (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform clients when correspondence received from the Office could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office (e.g., Office Actions, Final Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to inform clients of time-sensitive correspondence (e.g., a final rejection with a response deadline) constitutes a violation. The decision cites In re Van Der Wall as an example where failure to notify of a six-month response deadline led to a finding of violation. Treat such correspondence as time-sensitive and promptly communicate to the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence and adequate preparation (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b) and § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not handle a legal matter without 'preparation adequate in the circumstances' and must provide effective representation, acting with reasonable diligence and promptness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing documents without prudent preliminary steps or without adequately preparing (e.g., filing assignments or petitions without necessary research or authority) violates this duty. Examples include filing an application or amendment without consulting the client or failing to investigate whether paperwork can properly be filed. Neglect (failure to respond to Office correspondence leading to abandonment) is a breach of this competence/diligence duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely submission of required application components and fees (procedural filing obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patent and trademark filings, practitioners must submit required fees, oaths/declarations, powers of attorney, and replacement drawings within prescribed timeframes; Notices to File Missing Parts set deadlines and failure to comply may result in abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision recounts Notices to File Missing Parts and resulting Notices of Abandonment where fees or declarations were not timely paid or filed. Practitioners should monitor deadlines established by Notices and ensure client-paid fees are timely remitted or obtain client instructions to avoid abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling client funds and trust account obligations (37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(2),(3); § 11.115(a),(c),(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must identify and safekeep client property promptly, deposit client funds (including prepaid fees) into separate client trust accounts, disburse funds only as fees are earned and expenses incurred, and maintain complete records of all client funds, securities and other property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit client prepaid USPTO fees into client trust accounts (not general business or personal accounts); maintain ledgers, bank statements, canceled checks, transaction records, and separate listings of deposits identifying the client. Using client funds for unrelated personal expenses, mixing client and non-client funds, or allowing checks drawn on client funds to be dishonored violates these rules. Production of these records is expected in OED investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; such conduct evinces a lack of honesty, probity, or integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the regulations do not define these terms, the Court looks to common-law/dictionary definitions and prior case law. Examples: invoicing a client as if an office fee had been paid when it was not, and then using the client's payment for unrelated expenses — this can constitute misrepresentation/dishonesty. Misrepresentations involving client funds or filings are particularly serious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with OED investigations (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b)) and prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must cooperate with OED in investigations, respond to Requests for Information (RFIs), and produce requested documents; failure to cooperate is a violation and is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED may request client ledgers, bank records, canceled checks, deposit records, and explanations of trust account practices. Non-production or failure to respond to RFIs supports a finding of violation and aggravating conduct. Practitioners should timely and fully produce requested documents and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on use of catch‑all conduct provisions (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) and § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'catch-all' prohibiting other conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice cannot be applied where a more specific disciplinary rule already covers the conduct alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alleged conduct violates specific subsections (e.g., 10.23(b)(1)-(5)), it should not also be charged under the catch-all. Courts will not impose separate liability under the catch‑all when an applicable, more particular rule addresses the misconduct. Review prior decisions (In re Lane, In re Kelber) for application of this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions determination factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors govern sanctioning decisions: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) the practitioner's state of mind (intentional, knowing, or negligent); (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these factors to decide appropriate penalties (e.g., exclusion, suspension). Examples of aggravating factors include a pattern of misconduct across multiple matters/clients, refusal to cooperate with OED, continued misconduct after notice, and failure to acknowledge wrongdoing. The decision references the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when evaluating aggravating/mitigating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to suspend or exclude practitioners (35 U.S.C. § 32; applicable rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO, through the Director, has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for practice before it and to suspend or exclude persons shown to be incompetent, disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or in violation of Office regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary rules changed effective May 3, 2013: USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.100 et seq.) apply to conduct on/after that date; the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.) applies to earlier conduct. Remedies for exclusion or suspension are governed by regulations (e.g., 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60 regarding responsibilities after suspension/exclusion and petitions for reinstatement).
